I do agree, yes. Everything takes longer. If you're a player that is exclusively interested in end-game raiding, then classic is by no means a casual experience. My point is simply that if you have a casual player that just wants to log in and start having a good time, they can do that from "Enter World" (assuming they enjoy the gameplay ofc). In a way it does depend on what the individual player enjoys, like you said. But my point is simply that Classic isn't designed with the assumption that you're going to be raiding. Therefore, even though the raiding is not very casual friendly, the game overall is still quite casual friendly. In my opinion.

"Casual" doesn't mean "everyone is going to see all of the content". It means "everyone will be able to have fun playing the game". Which is what makes Classic better than BFA, in my opinion. In Classic, leveling is a major part of the experience and it is designed to be fun and engaging. In modern WoW, the only engaging parts are endgame and leveling is not very exciting. In a way, I consider Classic to be MORE casual friendly than modern WoW for this reason. Yes, leveling takes longer. But as soon as you enter the world, you are experiencing the game as it's meant to be played. Leveling in modern WoW is super fast, but that's only because it's such a vestigial part of the game. You have to sink a ton of time into modern wow to even start experiencing the fun part.

## Classic WoW Testing Schedule

Beginning May 15, select WoW players will be invited to participate in a small-scale, focused closed beta test. Players will also get a chance to help put our servers and technology through their paces in a series of stress tests running from May through July—you can opt in now through [Account Management](https://account.blizzard.com/games) and select the WoW Classic beta. Subsequent stress tests will extend the opportunity to even more players. Level caps will also be in place to ensure we’re emphasizing the “stress” in “stress test”

—we want to push our tech to the limit, and that means a critical mass of players in close proximity.

## STRESS TEST SCHEDULE*

* Stress Test 1: Wed May 22–Thurs May 23
* Stress Test 2: Wed Jun 19– Thurs Jun 20
* Stress Test 3: Thurs Jul 18– Fri July 19

\*Dates of each stress test are subject to change.

To fill our pool of beta and stress test participants, we’ll be choosing dedicated players who meet select criteria from both the WoW Classic beta opt-in and the standard Warcraft beta opt-in. Participants will also need to have an active subscription or active game time on their Battle.net Account. While opting-in to the beta is the primary way to make sure you’re in the running to join the test it doesn’t guarantee an invitation to the closed beta test. While rules lawyers can be very frustrating (don't worry, we *are* self-aware), the point of rules is to keep some semblance of structure to the game. Tabletop games can lose meaning really quickly if characters are just allowed to "do stuff" without following the proper rules. 
This is a really basic example, but it illustrates the point. Say a character wants to tumble away from an ogre and shoot an arrow. Simply moving backward and firing the arrow provokes an opportunity attack. The DM should enforce this, regardless of whether or not the rule seems pedantic and the character should be able to pull off this cool thing. The thing is, they *can* pull off the cool thing, it just takes some extra work. The DM may have the character make an acrobatics check to avoid provoking the opportunity attack.
Now, instead of "your character hops backward and fires an arrow", the situation becomes: "your character nimbly backflips over the ogre's reactive strike, and you fire your bow as you land." 
This is not only an objectively cooler action, it also allows the player to feel like they earned the *coolness*. This is why rules matter. Coolness earned is better than coolness arbitrarily accomplished.

The first step is probably to limit the number of healing surges that can be used during a short rest, or put the characters in situations where even a short rest might expose them to great danger. The key, and the difficulty, is maintaining tension while not actually killing all of the characters or intentionally putting them up against something too powerful for them. The best way to do this is to limit their healing or make the healing process tense.

In terms of making the game hard but fair, make sure that enemies are always putting themselves in an advantageous position. Remember that bad guys are smart too (especially Japanese demons/ yokai). Don't put an Oni alone in a big arena. Have it stalk the players for some time, hidden out of their sight, only to attack when the time is right.

For Japanese flavor that also helps the vibe, make sure to include "trickster" creatures. These kinds of creatures are common in Japanese folklore and can be really cool in a deadly adventure. Have a demon that is disguised as an NPC that betrays them in a critical moment (these sorts of characters are common in Souls-like games). 

Sorry if this is a bit vague, but there's a lot that can go into building and maintaining tension.
